transcript:
[00:00] Maya Patel: Hey everyone, thanks for joining — looks like we have a full house. Objective today is to decide whether Pegasus should go with a reserved GPU commit or rely on ephemeral burst capacity for your inference workloads. We pulled some traces ahead of time, thanks Evan.
[00:18] Rajesh Kumar: Yeah thanks, quick context — our core product does semi-realtime summarization for investor reports, latency target's 400ms p95 and we sometimes have spikes during earnings windows. We're sensitive to cost but can't miss SLA.
[00:34] Liam Ortega: Quick clarifying q — those 400ms p95 targets, are they end-to-end front-end to token or just inference?
[00:40] Tara Wilson: Inference only. We have edge caching but inference is the big cost.
[00:45] Liam Ortega: Got it. The tradeoff is pretty classic: reserved GPUs give predictable throughput and lower unit cost but require commit sizing; ephemeral/burst is great for spikes but can have cold-start/queue buildup and higher overall $/token. We'll walk through queueing models.
[01:05] Evan Ng: One of our constraints — the model needs KV cache per conversation. Warmup time for KV cache is about 200ms on average when moving to a new host. That matters for bursts.
[01:16] Sofia Reyes: Right, that 200ms KV warmup multiplies across concurrent sessions if you can't reuse host affinity. We suggested sticky-routing and warm pools to mitigate but that adds reserved capacity.
[01:29] Sasha: Sorry, sticky routing — that's per conversation pinning to a GPU? How does that scale when you have thousands of convos?
[01:35] Liam Ortega: We do per-session affinity with a TTL, so short lived sessions can reuse cache. For long tail, you either accept KV cache misses or hold reserved warm instances. There's a middle ground: tiny warm pool plus bursting ephemeral for heavy tails.
[01:50] Rajesh Kumar: Can you show the math on how queueing behaves under bursts? I saw your doc about M/M/c but our traffic isn't Poisson exactly.
[02:00] Liam Ortega: Totally — we can use an M/G/c approximation plus traces. In practice we run trace-driven sims — feed your arrival timestamps and model service times. For example, with 8 reserved A10-ish GPUs, sustained throughput is X tokens/s with KV hit ~85%, p95 sits around 360ms in our sim. If you remove reserved and go ephemeral-only, p95 jumps during 10x bursts because KV misses and container spin-up add latency.
[02:31] Tara Wilson: What about pre-warming ephemeral? Can we keep a tiny continuous fleet?
[02:35] Sofia Reyes: Yes — Redwood supports warm pools. The policy options are keep-alive pools, scale-to-zero with warmers (we run micro warmers that ping containers to keep KV initialized), and auto-warm based on scheduled events. Those warmers cost but are cheaper than full reserved commit.
[02:50] Evan Ng: But the concern is our compliance needs — if things run in Redwood hosted, data residency and audit logs are fine, but our security team wants VPC/private and HSM key access for model keys. Does private deployment support the same warm pool logic?
[03:05] Maya Patel: Yes, private (VPC) supports the same runtime features. The primary difference is who controls the infra; network egress and KMS integration are customer-managed. We'll share the VPC doc.
[03:15] Rajesh Kumar: Can you talk quantization? Tara has suggested 4-bit quant to double throughput but QA worries about quality delta.
[03:22] Liam Ortega: 4-bit (q4) can reduce memory and increase per-GPU throughput ~1.6-2x depending on kernel selection. But some models show generation artifacts at aggressive quant. Our recommendation is staged: run eval prompt set, check log-prob and hallucination metrics, and maybe use hybrid quant: q4 for most layers, higher precision for key layers. Also mixed-batch profiling helps.
[03:45] Tara Wilson: That hybrid approach sounds reasonable. Do you have automation to recommend quant profiles?
[03:49] Sofia Reyes: Redwood Optimize has a suggestion engine that looks at your workload distribution and suggests quant and batch sizes. We'll include an export with sample profiles.
[03:58] [05:00] Liam Ortega: Ok back to queueing, simple example: if arrival rate lambda is 100 req/s and a single GPU capacity mu is 25 req/s, with c=4 GPUs you barely match the mean; when spikes double, queue length grows nonlinearly. That's when backpressure helps — reject or queue with SLA-based admission. Redwood supports throttles per-route and token-bucket shaping.
[05:26] Evan Ng: We prefer graceful degradation over hard rejects — maybe reduce tokens or apply more aggressive quant on overflow?
[05:31] Liam Ortega: Exactly. Technique is dynamic model fallback and token reduction. For example, during pressure we route to a smaller model variant (distilled or q4) or reduce max_tokens. That keeps latency but might drop quality.
[05:46] Rajesh Kumar: How reliable are the fallbacks? If a fallback model is behind ephemeral capacity too, we could still be SORted.
[05:52] Sofia Reyes: You can define capacity rings: tier1 reserved for critical traffic, tier2 ephemeral for lower priority. Redwood's smart routing will attempt tier1 then fallback to tier2 and finally to a cheaper regional variant. You can also pin business-critical routes to reserved pools.
[06:10] Sasha: What's the economic break-even for reserved vs ephemeral? Can you show a worked example?
[06:14] Maya Patel: Sure — rough example: a reserved A10 pool at X $/hour yields Y tokens/sec cost of Z $/million tokens. Ephemeral average cost tends to be 20–40% higher if you rely heavily on bursts because you pay for spin-up inefficiencies and higher per-hour on-demand rates. But if your spikes are <10% of total traffic, ephemeral + warmers often win. We'll run your real numbers in a sim.
[06:40] Tara Wilson: Our spikes are about 18% of daily volume but concentrated in 4 earnings days per quarter. That 18% is big.
[06:48] Liam Ortega: For that pattern, reserved commit for a baseline plus burst capacity for earnings days is often optimal. You can also do seasonal reserved commits (3–6 month terms) to get discounts.
[06:58] Rajesh Kumar: Can you explain KV global caching — we've been thinking of doing global prefix caching so multiple GPUs can share KV. Is that supported?
[07:05] Sofia Reyes: Current runtime requires per-host KV in GPU memory for speed. There are hybrid approaches: shared KV storage with fast NVMe-backed caches or a federation layer that restores KV to the GPU more quickly during spin-up. But the fastest is host-local KV with affinity. We're prototyping cross-host KV warmers but it's not GA.
[07:26] Evan Ng: If we do host-local KV, how do we handle stateful routing when instances scale down?
[07:31] Liam Ortega: TTL-based affinity and sticky session mapping; when hosts scale down we drain sessions and write back minimal state. There's an operational tradeoff: draining delays scale-in but keeps latency low. You can set aggressive scale-in if you prefer cost savings.
[07:47] Rajesh Kumar: About batching — you typically recommend micro-batching at sub-50ms windows to increase throughput without hurting latency, right?
[07:54] Sofia Reyes: Exactly. Continuous batching groups concurrent requests within a small time window. For conversational workloads ~15–30ms batching window often gives big throughput wins with minimal added P50. But for p95-sensitive routes you might constrain batching and prefer pure single-request mode. Redwood gives per-route batching config.
[08:10] Tara Wilson: Do our traces show enough concurrency to benefit from batching during normal hours?
[08:14] Liam Ortega: Looking at the sample trace you provided (Evan's export), peak concurrency per second suggests batching could improve token throughput ~1.3x during day and ~2x during overnight batch windows. We'll put exact graphs in the simulation output.
[08:30] [09:00] Rajesh Kumar: One more on networking — if we run private (VPC) does the cross-AZ latency kill prompt throughput? Our infra team is worried.
[09:10] Maya Patel: Cross-AZ adds a few ms RTT; for token-level generation it's usually fine. For KV warmup across AZs it's more noticeable. In Private you control placement; we recommend collocating model pools with the closest app tier and using placement policies.
[09:25] Evan Ng: Do you support on-prem air-gapped? We have a compliance scenario to test next Q.
[09:30] Sofia Reyes: Yes, Redwood Private has an on-prem package. The runtime runs as containers; we provide an install bundle. Some features like hosted telemetry need different setup but core runtime, batching, and warm pools work. We'll share the ops checklist.
[09:44] Tara Wilson: Great. Back to open questions: we need a sim that uses our exact p95/p99 distributions and KV miss rates to see where break-even occurs.
[09:53] Liam Ortega: Agreed. Concrete plan: you send the last 30 days of arrival timestamps + per-request token lengths + observed KV hit/miss; we'll run a 24h sim with variants: (A) baseline reserved (N GPUs), (B) small reserved + warmers + ephemeral burst, (C) ephemeral-only with large warm pool. Output will include p50/p95/p99 latency estimates, cost estimations, and recommended reserved commit.
[10:14] Rajesh Kumar: For the sim, what model profiles will you use? Our prod model is a 7B transformer.
[10:19] Liam Ortega: We'll profile your 7B on an A100/MI250-ish baseline and also an optimized A10-like cheaper variant. We'll include quantization profiles q4/q8 and report quality delta on your evaluation prompts.
[10:30] Maya Patel: I'll own pricing comparisons and procurement notes. We'll also include a sample SLA/policy for canarying reserved commit and autoscale safety limits.
[10:39] Sasha: Who should I expect as the point of contact?
[10:42] Maya Patel: Me for commercial, Liam for technical sims. We'll follow up with calendar invites.
[10:47] [11:00] Tara Wilson: Any quick wins we can do while you run sims?
[11:03] Sofia Reyes: Yes — enable affinity for top10% sessions, reduce unnecessary max_tokens default, and try a conservative q8 quant in staging. We'll share exact CLI toggles.
[11:14] Maya Patel: Ok let's recap next steps — (1) Pegasus to provide traces and KV stats (Evan/Tara) (2) Redwood to run three sims + pricing (Liam/Maya) (3) Deliver VPC and on-prem docs + SOC2 appendix (Maya) (4) Follow up call to review sims and commit recommendation in early Jan.
[11:36] Rajesh Kumar: Sounds good, thanks everyone.
[11:40] [End of recording]
